alt="Sate Rep Marcus Evan speaks at the bill signing ceremony on Wednesday." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/70fb58b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6123x3436+0+323/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2F1a%2F212b407b2afa15dcb60c578df1df%2Fenergy-091621-07.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/036c1c5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6123x3436+0+323/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2F1a%2F212b407b2afa15dcb60c578df1df%2Fenergy-091621-07.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/70fb58b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6123x3436+0+323/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe3%2F1a%2F212b407b2afa15dcb60c578df1df%2Fenergy-091621-07.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>State Rep. Marcus Evans in 2021. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Gov. JB Pritzker has questioned who should investigate funeral homes given that his administration now only licenses the facilities, but he has said little else about what kind of legislative response should follow the horrors discovered at South Chicago Chapel.</p><p>Marsh said the solution typically thrown around in the wake of grisly incidents such as the one in the South Chicago Chapel is to pass stronger licensing laws, limiting who comes into the profession in the first place.</p><p>But bad actors, she said, are often already licensed. While the state had revoked South Chicago Chapel owner Clark Morgan’s license in 2024, his wife Johanna had retained her license.</p><p>“If we can't figure out how to head off people from engaging in this kind of behavior, then we have to have some sort of enforcement mechanism on the back end to try and figure it out before it's too late,” Marsh said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/11/south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home-bodies-mishandled-class-action-lawsuit" >Potential class-action lawsuit filed against South Deering funeral home for mishandling 56 bodies</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Michael D. Sharkey, an attorney who represents the Illinois Funeral Directors Association, said the group welcomes “fair and thoughtful regulation of funeral service.”</p><p>“Illinois has a lot of rules and regulations on the books concerning funeral homes and crematories,” Sharkey said. “[At South Chicago Chapel], I believe that this is a failure of state agencies to properly enforce those and to properly track the alleged nefarious characters.”</p><h3>Pritzker hints at oversight changes</h3><p>The state Department of Financial and Professional Regulation said it received a tip about “potential operation concerns” at the South Chicago Chapel, prompting Chicago police to investigate and uncover more than 50 unrefrigerated bodies at various stages of decomposition.</p><p>Prior to that tip, what had been going on at the funeral home had gone unnoticed by the state.</p><p>But some elected officials, including Pritzker, are questioning whether the state Department of Financial and Professional Regulation is the right avenue to handle complaints of potential abuses. The governor said he’s meeting with Comptroller Susana Mendoza’s office about possibly streamlining how complaints are reported to the state.</p><p>“IDFPR is a licensing organization, but the investigatory endeavor — we should all discuss whether that's something that should belong to IDFPR or to some other body,” Pritzker said.</p><p> On Monday, WBEZ sought clarity from Pritzker’s office on that comment and asked whether the governor favored regular funeral home inspections by the state, tougher criminal penalties for desecrating human remains inside funeral homes or creation of a blue-ribbon panel to propose tougher oversight measures for funeral homes.</p><p>A Pritzker spokesperson declined comment.</p><p>Thirty-six other states have created separate funeral boards to manage director licenses, funeral homes, crematories and cemeteries. The other 14 states, excluding Illinois, have appointed state agencies, such as public health departments, to the task.</p><p>Creating a unified board is something state Rep. Diane Blair-Sherlock, D-Villa Park, is considering. She chairs the House State Government Administration Committee, which typically handles funeral home legislation, and worked on the bill granting the comptroller more regulatory powers over cemeteries.</p><p>But Blair-Sherlock said she’s not sure if the comptroller or the IDFPR have the resources to become the state’s one-stop-shop for funeral industry oversight.</p><p>“Sometimes we want to give it to a department, and the department says we're not equipped for that,” Blair Sherlock said. “I believe that we will be able to do something early next year.”</p><p>And while a vast majority of other states carry out annual or bi-annual inspections of funeral homes, sometimes even unannounced searches, Illinois is one of four states — along with Alaska, Hawaii and Iowa — that do not conduct any inspections of licensed funeral homes, crematories or cemeteries.</p><p>Starting next year, the comptroller’s office will have authority to inspect cemeteries only after a complaint has been filed.</p><p>“The tragic situation that happened in Chicago, this is not a number of bodies that piled up in the last week, right?” Marsh said. “The more frequent inspections are by the state, the more likely they are to catch this kind of problem before it gets completely out of hand.”</p><p>A spokeswoman for Mendoza said she is also looking at implementing harsher criminal penalties for funeral directors who mishandle human remains following what happened at South Chicago Chapel.</p><p>“Comptroller Mendoza believes these people belong in jail,” Mendoza spokeswoman Kim Howard said.</p><p> In 2024, Pritzker signed legislation that imposed new criminal penalties against funeral home operators who knowingly made false statements on death certificates, kept false records or maintained ill-equipped preparation rooms where bodies are prepared for burial.</p><p>There was no language in that law that explicitly imposed criminal penalties for the desecration of bodies inside funeral homes.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://illinoiscomptroller.gov/newsroom/press-releases/comptroller-mendoza-permanently-closes-heights-crematory-through-consent-order" target="_blank" ><u>In June 2025</u></a>, Mendoza’s office revoked the chapel’s crematory license, and handed over evidence of the owners improperly storing remains to the Cook County State’s Attorney's office and the Illinois State Police. Neither Clark nor Johanna Morgan were arrested.</p><p>Howard said the goal is to introduce legislation with tougher criminal penalties for funeral home operators during the fall veto session, which begins in mid-November.</p><h3><b>Lawmaker says state ‘not on top of this’</b></h3><p>Illinois has seen high-profile cases of funeral and cemetery directors mishandling human remains over the past 15 years.</p><p>In 2024, a downstate funeral home was found by authorities to have misidentified up to 800 cremated ashes. That triggered passage of a law requiring crematories to affix remains with a unique ID and maintain chain-of-custody documentation.</p><p>And in 2009, the Cook County Sheriff’s office found former Burr Oak Cemetery manager Carolyn Towns and three other workers had dug up graves, dumped the bodies and resold plots. The workers were later convicted, and Towns got a 12-year prison sentence.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7e0000" name="image-7e0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5e26e64/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2784x1562+0+143/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2Fdd%2Ff82eb0e71069cc41c7fd5df643bc%2Fburroak-cst-012915-10-600x398.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c1749a4/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2784x1562+0+143/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2Fdd%2Ff82eb0e71069cc41c7fd5df643bc%2Fburroak-cst-012915-10-600x398.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f369233/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2784x1562+0+143/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2Fdd%2Ff82eb0e71069cc41c7fd5df643bc%2Fburroak-cst-012915-10-600x398.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Rows of tombstones at the Burr Oak Cemetery in 2009. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f369233/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2784x1562+0+143/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2Fdd%2Ff82eb0e71069cc41c7fd5df643bc%2Fburroak-cst-012915-10-600x398.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9a9e35c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2784x1562+0+143/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2Fdd%2Ff82eb0e71069cc41c7fd5df643bc%2Fburroak-cst-012915-10-600x398.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f369233/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2784x1562+0+143/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F02%2Fdd%2Ff82eb0e71069cc41c7fd5df643bc%2Fburroak-cst-012915-10-600x398.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Rows of tombstones at the Burr Oak Cemetery in 2009. Four cemetery workers were charged with dismembering human remains. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file photo</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The historic, predominantly African-American cemetery in Alsip, which is the final resting place for slain civil rights icon Emmett Till, singer Dinah Washington and bluesman Willie Dixon, is now under new ownership</p><p>In response, then-Gov. Pat Quinn assembled a bipartisan task force of state lawmakers to come up with legislation clamping down on cemeteries.</p><p>Former Republican State Rep. Dan Brady, R-Bloomington, was one of those lawmakers. Brady is now mayor of Bloomington and a longtime funeral director.</p><p>“The situation I experienced as a legislator on that task force was consumers that testified before us that had suspicions of things, whether that be at a funeral home, at a cemetery… didn't know where to turn,” Brady said.</p><p>He and the task force recommended the legislature consolidate all funeral and burial oversight under the state Department of Financial and Professional Regulation and enact a law mandating cemetery managers be licensed.</p><p>Quinn signed the latter mandating cemetery management licensure into law in 2010. But the other bill consolidating funeral home and cemetery oversight <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus/FullText?GAID=10&DocNum=5159&DocTypeID=HB&LegId=50095&SessionID=76" target="_blank" ><u>stalled</u></a>.</p><p>“There were opposing folks in the industry that felt that leaving things to the status quo was better,” Brady said. “[For] those of us who sat on the task force to listen to testimony, that was just the opposite. We wouldn't have Burr Oak… if we had some of those recommendations maybe back then.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-840000" name="image-840000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/943b138/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F20%2Fb8%2Fd7485b9b13a3bd7879f6f66c56cc%2Fbrady-061722-3.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c6494f3/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F20%2Fb8%2Fd7485b9b13a3bd7879f6f66c56cc%2Fbrady-061722-3.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0c49fc0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F20%2Fb8%2Fd7485b9b13a3bd7879f6f66c56cc%2Fbrady-061722-3.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="State Rep. Dan Brady (R-Bloomington), the GOP candidate for Illinois secretary of state." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0c49fc0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F20%2Fb8%2Fd7485b9b13a3bd7879f6f66c56cc%2Fbrady-061722-3.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9e0bb90/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F20%2Fb8%2Fd7485b9b13a3bd7879f6f66c56cc%2Fbrady-061722-3.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0c49fc0/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F20%2Fb8%2Fd7485b9b13a3bd7879f6f66c56cc%2Fbrady-061722-3.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Former state Rep. Dan Brady, shown in 2022. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file photo</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Now six years later, Rep. Evans is joining Blair-Sherlock and other Democratic members in calling for new legislation that would consolidate oversight of funeral homes and cemeteries under one state body. Evans said passing funeral home oversight reforms in recent years “just hasn’t been a priority, for whatever reason.”</p><p>And for that, Evans is apologetic.</p><p>“I’m sorry for the loved ones that we were not on top of this,” he said. “But there’s a game plan now. We don't want bad actors to feel any comfort with regards to abusing the remains of our loved ones.”</p>

entries.title: Noah Properties to finish 354 luxury apartments at former White Eagle site in 2027
entries.summary: <p>The largest development project in Niles is transforming what was once a mecca for Chicago’s Polish community into hundreds of new units of housing.</p><p>Village officials said the Riverbank, a 10-building residential project at the former White Eagle Events and Convention Center, is expected to finish December 2027.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/curious-city/2016/09/18/the-making-of-polish-chicago" target="_blank" >White Eagle</a> — which cost $250,000 to demolish — was a staple among Polish families for funeral receptions, baptisms and other gatherings. The venue, 6839 N. Milwaukee Ave., hosted dignitaries spanning from former President Jimmy Carter to Pope John Paul II and Muhammad Ali. Poland's former President Lech Wałęsa also visited the White Eagle. It was also located across from St. Adalbert Cemetery, a Catholic — and largely Polish — burial site.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/12/29/developer-noah-properties-apartments-white-eagle-niles" >$156 million Riverbank</a> project is complete, Niles officials said the gateway will be revitalized with art, much-needed housing and public green space.</p><p>“What you’re going to see along Milwaukee Avenue is transformation,” Chris Ragusto, Niles’ director of community development, said.</p><p>Developing the Riverbank is Noah Properties, led by Bart Przyjemski. Przyjemski is a native of Poland and a former Niles resident. He purchased the site in December 2025 for $5.7 million, with a $3.9 million mortgage from California-based Genesis Capital, property records show.</p><p>The Riverbank will have 354 luxury units including studios, one-, two- and four-bedroom homes. Pricing hasn't been determined. The site, spanning 7 acres, will also have a new park, public plaza, pool, playground and parking.</p><p>Construction has been ongoing for the past six months, according to village officials. In July, developers hit a major milestone: framing for the six rows of townhomes was completed. Some of the first townhomes have their windows installed, with interior finishes underway. By the end of August, crews will begin installing drywall, tile and flooring in some of the first units.</p><p>Steel framing is going up on one the apartment buildings, while a second apartment building has its foundation for the attached parking garage poured.</p><p>And where the White Eagle used to sit is a giant excavated hole, at least until construction starts at that portion of the site. The developer is still waiting on permit approvals for buildings planned at the front of the property. The medical building at 6759 N. Milwaukee has been vacated, and it will eventually be demolished.</p><p>Niles Mayor George Alpogianis said the Riverbank will help usher in the next chapter for the site. The apartments and townhomes will attract young professionals and families, who may not be ready or have the money to buy a home yet, but still want to be in Niles for its location, schools and public libraries, he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-570000" name="image-570000"></a> project.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>There’s great demand for high-end luxury rental units in Niles, Alpogianis said. For example, Novu, a new luxury 180-unit apartment at 6633 N. Milwaukee that was developed by Noah Properties, is 80% leased. And the luxury apartment building The Grand Stone, 9201 N. Milwaukee, leased all its 48 units in one month, according to Ragusto.</p><p>The White Eagle <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/11/19/white-eagle-banquets-in-niles-to-close-at-end-of-year" >closed</a> at the end of 2025. Ted Przybylo opened the business in 1947 and moved it from Chicago to Niles in 1967.</p><p>The White Eagle’s nearly 60-year run was “so monumental” for Niles and those who frequented it, including much of Chicago’s Democratic Party, Alpogianis said. But there’s no longer a need for a roughly 1,000-seat banquet hall like the White Eagle.</p><p>“As much as we worked with [the owners] to try and figure things out and try to reimagine the White Eagle, it unfortunately had its day,” Alpogianis said.</p><p>The White Eagle site is one the village “wanted to pay particular attention to,” Ragusto said. </p><p>Niles' South Milwaukee Avenue Corridor Plan calls for widening Milwaukee Avenue, which Noah Properties will undertake along with new landscaping and an art plaza. And the Niles 2040 Comprehensive Plan, adopted in 2024, calls for more places for residents. The 2040 plan also envisions Milwaukee Avenue as a place where residents can live, work, shop and play.</p><p>Remembering the history of the White Eagle is important as the Milwaukee Avenue parcel evolves, officials said.</p><p>The Niles Historical Society took a “number of items” from the banquet hall prior to demolition, Katie Schneider, deputy village manager of Niles, said. The items will likely be housed at The Niles Historical and Cultural Center, where they will help tell the story of Polish immigrants in the village. But it’s possible they’re repurposed on the property, along with stained glass and original cladding from the former Silver Leaf Tavern that once stood on the site.</p><p>“The Polish community has just been such a part of our history, and that's a large part because of the White Eagle,” Schneider said. “The bread-and-butter of Niles is our small businesses and people that come here to build and truly live the American dream. And they have family-owned businesses — that's what the White Eagle really was.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/12/29/developer-noah-properties-apartments-white-eagle-niles" >Developer plans 354 apartments at White Eagle site in Niles</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/11/19/white-eagle-banquets-in-niles-to-close-at-end-of-year" >White Eagle banquets in Niles to close at end of year</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: ESPN co-founder Bill Rasmussen dies at 93 from the effects of Parkinson’s disease
entries.summary: <p>LAND O’ LAKES, Fla. (AP) — Bill Rasmussen, who co-founded ESPN in 1979 after being fired from a public relations job in the World Hockey Association, died Tuesday. He was 93.</p><p>ESPN historian Mike Soltys said Rasmussen died at his Florida home from the effects of Parkinson’s disease. Rasmussen announced in 2019 that he had been diagnosed with the degenerative disease in 2014.</p><p>“Bill was a remarkable man — a visionary and an innovator who conceived the idea of a network entirely devoted to sports,” ESPN chairman Jimmy Pitaro said in a statement. “Quite simply, none of us would be here today if it wasn’t for Bill’s passion and all the hard work and entrepreneurial spirit he put into building ESPN in the late 1970s — key aspects of our company culture that still carry on to this day.”</p><p>Rasmussen and his son Scott came up with the idea of a network carrying sports around the clock, and it would revolutionize Americans’ TV-watching habits. But the pair didn’t stick around long. They were forced out after only a year by ESPN majority owner Getty Oil.</p><p>Bill Rasmussen’s original idea was a cable channel covering only Connecticut sports. Many cable operators in the state were skeptical, but someone suggested buying satellite time to reach a national audience.</p><p>ESPN was launched on Sept. 7, 1979. George Grande welcomed viewers to the first “SportsCenter” broadcast before the network’s first live event, a slow-pitch softball game between the Kentucky Bourbons and the Milwaukee Schlitz.</p><p>“In those days, we didn’t know if we’d last four weeks, four years, let alone 40-some, but we knew it was special,” Grande said. “Bottom line was Bill Rasmussen was the true pervader of the original American dream, and he gave us all something very special that we still have today.”</p><p>The Rasmussens secured financial backing from Getty Oil and a rights deal with the NCAA, and built a studio in Bristol, Connecticut, still under construction when ESPN went on the air.</p><p>The Getty investment and the deal with the NCAA occurred on the same day.</p><p>“When someone tells you you can’t do something, you want to prove them wrong,” Bill Rasmussen said. “Many, many people told us there wasn’t enough sports to do a 24-hour channel. I didn’t argue with anybody. I just thought they were wrong and I was right.”</p><p>When the Rasmussens were forced out of ESPN in 1980, Getty owned 85% of the network. Texaco, which had acquired Getty, sold its interest in ESPN to ABC in 1984.</p><p>Bill Rasmussen and ESPN were estranged until 1999, when company executives invited him to the 20th anniversary celebration. Since then, he has been embraced and recognized for his vision of creating an all-sports network. He toured the country in 2019 for the 40th anniversary and gave speeches at Walt Disney Co. and ESPN events.</p><p>“Bill was our George Washington and a good friend,” said veteran anchor Chris Berman, who joined ESPN three weeks after the network launched in 1979. “He was such a grateful person and every sports fan can be grateful for Bill. He wasn’t a glass half-full guy; his glass was always overflowing with optimism. He greeted everyone with a smile and we can all smile knowing Bill’s legacy.”</p><p>Born in Chicago, Rasmussen earned degrees from DePauw University in Indiana and Rutgers University and served in the Air Force. He started an advertising services business, then worked in radio and television as a broadcaster during the 1960s.</p><p>He was hired in 1974 as public relations director for the WHA’s New England Whalers in Hartford, Connecticut. The team’s entire front office was fired in 1978, and Rasmussen soon turned his attention to brainstorming with his son on the creation of sports on cable TV with the help of a $9,000 credit card advance.</p><p>“There was a whole lot of chutzpah and a whole lot of vision, and they’re maxed out on their credit cards. It’s the American dream,” said Bob Ley, one of the network’s original anchors.</p><p>Rasmussen was inducted into the Sports Broadcasting Hall of Fame in 2025.</p><p>Rasmussen was predeceased by his wife of 56 years, Lois, in 2011 and is survived by two sons, Scott Rasmussen and his wife, Laura, and Glenn Rasmussen, daughter Lynn Van Hollebeke and her husband, Louie, seven grandchildren, one great-grandson and one great-granddaughter. In addition to his wife, Bill was predeceased by his brothers Robert and Donald Rasmussen, sister Vivien and a grandson.</p>

entries.title: Pumpkins, pensions, and the CTU's 'cooked' books
entries.summary: <p>Is criticism a crime?</p><p>As fond as I am of teachers, generally, and despite being a good union man myself, I couldn't help but shake my head in wonder at the Chicago Teachers Union, which I consider a fairly savvy organization, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/08/17/chicago-teachers-union-illinois-policy-institute-defamation-lawsuit-stacy-davis-gates" >suing a pair of conservative watchdogs,</a> the Illinois Policy Institute and the Liberty Justice Center, for sinking their teeth into CTU finances and accusing the union of using "cooked" books.</p><p>First, way to turn a spotlight on their accusations. Believe it or not, I'm not checking the <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoispolicy.org/illinois-grows-enough-pumpkins-for-8b-pumpkin-spice-lattes/" target="_blank" >Illinois Policy Institute website</a> every morning to see what's in their crosshairs. Doing that, right now, I see their top story is on ... pumpkins. "The state produces enough pumpkins to make nearly 8 billion pumpkin spice lattes, the most pumpkins in the U.S." At first I thought it must be a mistake — the colorful, pumpkin-centric page labeled "Illinois Policy" must be different from "Illinois Policy Institute."</p><p>Nope. Same folks.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fd0000" name="module-fd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>But is it true? <a class="Link" href="https://www.blogger.com/blog/post/edit/3972382144120426476/4857837068088532900#" target="_blank" >According to the United States Department of Agriculture</a>, the top producer of pumpkins in the country is ... Illinois, head and shoulders above the rest, responsible for 40% of all the big orange squashes grown nationwide.</p><p>Did you know that? I did not. Score one for the Illinois Policy Institute.</p><p>The second story "CHICAGO TEACHERS UNION UNDERMINES YET ANOTHER CHARTER SCHOOL" begins: "The Chicago Teachers Union’s relentless attacks on charter schools has claimed another victim. The Chicago High School for the Arts announced it will not renew its contract with Chicago Public Schools, citing financial struggles. It will stop operations at the end of the current 2025-2026 school year."</p><p>Is that true? Kinda. The charter school will stop operations, but the school itself will transition into a public school. You could also say ... as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/07/30/chiarts-funding-vote-postponed-as-cps-board-debates-budget-consequences" target="_blank" >a Sun-Times story</a> suggested last month ... that CPS stepped in and saved the school after its charter operators decided to abandon it, one of the many downsides of privatizing public education. As a rule, the Chicago Public Schools are not shutting down schools willy-nilly, at least not since Rahm Emanuel left office.</p><p>That said, with Republicans dwelling in a near hallucinatory fantasy world where elections they lose are by definition fraudulent and along with inconvenient timbers of the Constitution can simply be wished away, I'd say that any thinking that bears even a rough resemblance to reality ought to be encouraged. So yes, just as the teachers union is opposed to charter schools, viewing them as corporate dodges to get around union protections, so the IPI is for them, as part of the parental choice/school voucher canard designed to direct public money into private pockets. Let the best man win.</p><p></p><p>Spin aside, I'm learning stuff. Honestly, quite an attractive website. I'll have to add it to my list.</p><p>The third story, "WITHOUT REFORMS, PENSION INSOLVENCY WILL EAT CHICAGO ALIVE," well, hard to argue that one. I've said for years that the city slides toward becoming one vast pension fund that also puts out fires. Maybe the CTU will sue me next.</p><p>Not to give them ideas. Back to suing Illinois Policy Institute. Bush league move. Did the CTU ever pause to wonder how this makes them look? Spend any time communicating in public and people are going to attack you. If I sued everyone who accused me of simply parroting whatever George Soros instructs me to say, I'd spend all my time in court.</p><p>Speaking of court. Since the lawsuit pivots on charges that the CTU "cooked" their books, doesn't this lawsuit invite the Illinois Policy Institute to pick over the union's finances with a lice comb, and show up in court with all sorts of charts highlighting every error, discrepancy and questionable meal expense they can find? Isn't that exactly what the IPI wants to do anyway? And isn't the CTU basically shining klieg lights, setting the stage for the IPI to parade their charges and theories across? I think they are.</p><p>In checking out the Illinois Policy Institute's reputation, I found a 2018 article that says this about the organization:</p><p>"Its studies and opinion pieces on cutting government spending and boosting transparency became must-read material to many Republicans, some Democrats," Mick Dumke and Tina Sfondeles wrote in the Sun-Times, while pointing out that its operator, John Tillman, was raking in millions.</p><p>"As the institute attacked political insiders for profiting off the system, Tillman parlayed its small-government message into growing paychecks for himself and other top staff members, tax filings and audits show," the paper wrote.</p><p>Though the story questioned the legality of what the Illinois Policy Institute was doing, its leaders did not sue the Sun-Times. What do they know that the Chicago Teachers Union doesn't?</p>
entries.author: Neil Steinberg

entries.title: Bears coach: RB Kyle Monangai 'week-to-week' after hurting knee
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> running back <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/16/bears-training-camp-kyle-monangai-right-knee-injury-practice" target="_blank" >Kyle Monangai</a> seems to have avoided the worst-case scenario.</p><p>Coach Ben Johnson said Tuesday that he will be "week-to-week" with a knee injury that he suffered Sunday when he got tangled up with defensive tackle Grady Jarrett during a drill in which neither of them were wearing full pads. </p><p>The injury could have been much worse. Monangai limped off the field and Jarrett was emotional about the collision.</p><p>Johnson said Tuesday that he didn't need to have a conversation with Jarrett, who is entering his 12th season in the NFL and second with the Bears.</p><p>Roschon Johnson and Salvon Ahmed had been behind Monangai during training camp and figure to get the majority of his work in the weeks moving forward. Johnson led the team in carries and rushing yards Saturday against the Browns, while Ahmed scored on a 49-yard screen pass.</p><p>The Bears' season opener is more than 3 1/2 weeks away.</p><p></p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Detienen a 16 adolescentes en el abandonado y clausurado Congress Theater luego de un rave ilegal
entries.summary: <p>Dieciséis adolescentes fueron arrestados en el Congress Theater la noche del viernes, casi una semana después de que la policía clausurara un rave no autorizado en el local cerrado del vecindario de Logan Square.</p><p>La Policía de Chicago dijo que los agentes respondieron a una llamada por invasión de propiedad privada a eso de las 8:15 p.m. el viernes en la cuadra 2100 al norte de Milwaukee Avenue. Cuando los agentes entraron al teatro, varias personas intentaron huir.</p><p>Los 16 adolescentes, de entre 13 y 19 años, fueron imputados cada uno por un delito menor de allanamiento, según la policía. Cuatro fueron acusados de conducta temeraria y a dos se les impuso una citación por portar pistolas de balines.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-050000" name="module-050000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>El arresto masivo ocurrió después de que un DJ local organizara un rave ilegal en el teatro el 8 de agosto que atrajo a varios jóvenes, según Block Club Chicago. Llamaron a la policía para clausurarla, pero los agentes no arrestaron a ninguno de los asistentes.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/01/14/landmark-congress-theater-federal-loan-preservation-finance-committee-city-council" target="_blank" >Hay planes para rehabilitar</a> el Congress Theater, que ha permanecido vacante desde 2013. Con un préstamo federal de $25.2 millones y subvenciones de la Ciudad, los constructores inmobiliarios detrás de la renovación planean volver a convertir el teatro en un espacio de entretenimiento y añadir locales comerciales, oficinas y viviendas.</p><p>En su boletín semanal, el concejal Daniel La Spata (1.º) condenó el rave y dijo que retrasó el esfuerzo de rehabilitación.</p><p>"Los participantes causaron daños significativos al edificio, aumentando sustancialmente el costo de su rehabilitación", escribió La Spata. El rave también "requirió una respuesta policial que distrajo la atención de asuntos mucho más importantes".</p><p>El domingo, La Spata no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: CTA adding 4 bus routes to Frequent Network
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Transit Authority is adding 10-minutes-or-better service to four more bus routes, further expanding its Frequent Network that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/03/03/cta-frequent-network-bus-service" target="_blank" >launched last year</a>.</p><p>The Frequent Network will expand starting Sunday to three more lines: the No. 35 31st/35th, No. 74 Fullerton and No. 85 Central. In December, the No. 8 Halsted route will be added. </p><p>When complete, the expansion will bring 24 total bus routes to the Frequent Network, which provides service every 10 minutes or better on weekdays from 6 a.m. and 9 p.m., and on weekends from 9 a.m. and 9 p.m.</p><p>Unrelated to the Frequent Network, the CTA also is adding more buses to seven other routes by the end of the year:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-2f415152-9b1e-11f1-a18c-bd35dd6cbed1"><li>No. 3 King Drive: Earlier Sunday/holiday service</li><li>No. 44 Wallace/Racine: Earlier Sunday/holiday service</li><li>No. 70 Division: Earlier weekday service</li><li>No. 74 Fullerton: More frequent service between 9 p.m. and midnight on weekends</li><li>No. 73 Armitage: Later Saturday and Sunday service</li><li>No. 76 Diversey: Earlier Sunday/holiday service, later Saturday and Sunday/holiday service</li><li>No. 91 Austin: Earlier Saturday and Sunday/holiday service</li></ul><p>The extra scheduled buses — many of them during midday, evening and weekend hours — are supported by new funding from the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2025/12/16/illinois-transit-bill-signed-pritzker" target="_blank" >landmark Northern Illinois Transit Authority Act</a>, according to the CTA.</p><p>The CTA said the network provides strong connections to sister agencies Pace and Metra, a requirement of the NITA law that aims to improve coordination between the agencies. The law requires all three agencies to have a unified fare system by 2030.</p><p>By the end of the year, 75% of the CTA's service area will be within a half-mile of a frequent bus route, according to the agency.</p><p>The other current routes that are part of the Frequent Network are:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-69388802-9b1f-11f1-88e8-5db2ce564d39"><li>No. 4 Cottage Grove</li><li>No. entries.title: Man critically wounded in Near West Side shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man was critically wounded in a shooting early Tuesday on the Near West Side. </p><p>The 28-year-old was found in the first block of North Leavitt Street about 3:05 a.m. and taken to Stroger Hospital where he was in critical condition, police said. </p><p>Area 3 detectives were investigating.</p>

entries.title: Acusan de delitos de drogas a hombre que era perseguido por la oficial de la Policía de Chicago Krystal Rivera
entries.summary: <p>El hombre al que la oficial de la Policía de Chicago, Krystal Rivera, perseguía cuando fue fatalmente baleada por su compañero el año pasado, fue imputado por cargos de conspiración para traficar fentanilo y cocaína en Chicago, informó la oficina del fiscal federal.</p><p>Rivera y el oficial Carlos Baker persiguieron a Jaylin Arnold hasta un apartamento en el vecindario de Chatham en junio de 2025, donde Baker disparó su arma, hiriendo y matando a Rivera. Arnold se declaró culpable de cargos relacionados con armas y drogas por la muerte de Rivera y fue sentenciado a ocho años de prisión como parte del acuerdo de culpabilidad, sentencia que Yolanda Rivera, la madre de Krystal, calificó de "extremadamente severa".</p><p>Arnold, de 28 años, fue imputado el jueves por un gran jurado federal por tráfico de drogas presuntamente realizado junto con otros cuatro hombres entre enero y junio de 2025, según la acusación.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fd0000" name="module-fd0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Yolanda Rivera presentó una demanda por la muerte injusta contra Baker y el Departamento de Policía de Chicago (CPD), alegando que, al momento en que le disparó a su hija, Baker tenía dificultades para aceptar que Krystal Rivera había terminado su relación romántica con él. El Sun-Times y el Illinois Answers Project hallaron que Baker tenía un extenso historial disciplinario con más de una docena de denuncias por mala conducta.</p><p>La demanda afirma que Krystal Rivera amenazó con contarle a la novia con la que Baker vivía sobre su relación, y luego lo dejó. El día antes del tiroteo, Baker se presentó sin invitación en la casa de Krystal Rivera, según la demanda.</p><p>Después de que Arnold se declarara culpable de los cargos de drogas y armas relacionados con la muerte de su hija, Yolanda Rivera dijo que él "merece una sentencia que refleje la verdad de su papel, no la carga de fallas institucionales fuera de su control".</p><p>En el momento del acuerdo, el abogado de Arnold, Michael Clancy, destacó que es importante no confundir los cargos de armas de Arnold con la muerte de Krystal Rivera. "Creo que todos deben recordar que no fue acusado por la muerte de la oficial por haber tenido algo que ver con causar la muerte de la oficial", dijo Clancy.</p><p>Tras el único disparo de Baker que alcanzó a Krystal Rivera, el oficial esperó más de 90 segundos para prestar auxilio mientras ella jadeaba por aire, según la demanda y las imágenes de la cámara corporal.</p><p>"El oficial no prestó ayuda cuando era gravemente necesario", dijo Yolanda Rivera en la corte cuando Arnold se declaró culpable. "Es difícil aceptar que Arnold deba llevar el peso".</p><p>Arnold fue condenado previamente a siete años de prisión tras ser declarado culpable de cargos relacionados con armas en 2023 y ha sido sentenciado al menos en dos ocasiones más por cargos de armas.</p><p>Clancy no respondió de inmediato a las solicitudes de comentario sobre la acusación.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Banda punk de jóvenes de La Villita gana primer lugar en concurso de Riot Fest y tocará en el festival
entries.summary: <p>Fue una tarde gris, pero eso no impidió que residentes de North Lawndale y La Villita acudieran a la celebración de fin de verano organizada por la concejal Monique Scott (24.°) en Douglass Park.</p><p>Ese parque pronto será la sede de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/05/28/tool-twenty-one-pilots-pierce-the-veil-alanis-morissette-morrissey-riot-fest-lineup" target="_blank" >Riot Fest</a>, el festival de música de tres días que este año se realizará del 18 al 20 de septiembre.</p><p>La presentación en vivo se organizó en colaboración con el festival, que cada otoño atrae a miles de aficionados del punk rock a la zona. A comienzos del verano, la oficina de Scott y Riot Fest lanzaron una convocatoria para que bandas comunitarias enviaran su música y tuvieran la oportunidad de actuar en el festival de septiembre.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-870000" name="module-870000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Más de 100 agrupaciones locales solicitaron la oportunidad, pero sólo nueve fueron seleccionadas para la muestra de talento, en la que competirían por el codiciado lugar en el programa de 2026, que incluye como líderes del programa a Twenty One Pilots, Tool y Pierce the Veil.</p><p>El concurso de bandas locales forma parte de la iniciativa “Beyond the Fest”, lanzada en 2023 para ayudar a calmar las tensiones con sus vecinos por el uso de Douglass Park, un espacio verde clave en la comunidad.</p><p>Entre los talentos estuvieron algunos ganadores previos del concurso de bandas comunitarias: VII (Seven), ganadora de 2024, y NewClear Fusion, de 2023. También participaron las bandas locales Rose of Demise, Mother of Fortune, Large Mouth, Through N Through, William Baranda y su banda, Fantasma Negra y LP Trixie.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT for Teens, promising a more age-appropriate chatbot
entries.summary: <p>OpenAI is launching a version of ChatGPT designed for teenagers — the first generation to grow up with artificial intelligence — who are already using it for schoolwork, questions about daily life and even companionship.</p><p>The San Francisco-based company said ChatGPT for Teens, which launched Tuesday, is tailored for kids aged 13 to 17 with stronger protections including content restrictions around things like suicide, self-harm and romantic or sexual chats. It also provides homework and study support designed to help students learn rather than spit out answers and school essays.</p><p>The idea is to guide teens toward healthy AI use in an age-appropriate environment, the company said.</p><p>“We want to treat teens like teens, which means that we have to make sure that we’re showing up with the right developmental stage when we’re not either talking down to them or treating them like kids, but we’re also making sure that they’re not exposed to material that they shouldn’t be exposed to,” Ann O'Leary, vice president of global policy at OpenAI, said.</p><p>Parents, educators and child development experts have been sounding alarms over children's use of AI chatbots, which have been blamed for facilitating cheating on schoolwork and even suicide. And while even adults can fall victim to anthropomorphizing AI and developing unhealthy relationships with it, teenagers' brains are not yet fully developed and they can be particularly vulnerable.</p><p>Last year, research from a watchdog group found that ChatGPT would tell 13-year-olds how to get drunk and high, instruct them on how to conceal eating disorders and even compose a heartbreaking suicide letter to their parents if asked. In interactions with researchers posing as vulnerable teens, ChatGPT typically warned against risky activity but went on to deliver startlingly detailed and personalized plans for drug use, calorie-restricted diets or self-injury.</p><p>In the U.S., more than 70% of teens are turning to AI chatbots for companionship and half use AI companions regularly, according to a 2025 study from Common Sense Media, a group that studies and advocates for using digital media sensibly.</p><p>OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has said that the company is trying to study “emotional overreliance” on the technology, describing it last year as a “really common thing” with young people.</p><p>For users of ChatGPT for Teens, the chatbot is prevented from suggesting it has personal feelings toward the user or implying that it is conscious or experiences emotions, according to OpenAI. That's in addition to blocking romantic or sexual chats.</p><p>“We went through and identified what are the hypothetical cues that a model could give that might make a teenager kind of develop a relationship to it,” Allison Mishkin, head of child development at OpenAI, said.</p><p>OpenAI doesn't verify users' ages, but it already uses age assurance to estimate if someone is under 18 based on factors such as their types of queries. If someone is identified or identifies themselves as a minor, they are automatically placed into the teen version of the chatbot. This is similar to Meta's approach to teen accounts on Instagram, which have stricter content, chat and privacy restrictions than regular accounts.</p><p>To use parental controls, both the teen user and their parent or guardian have to opt in. But O'Leary said the idea with the teen chatbot is to “make sure that this is safe, even if you don’t use parental controls.” Parents with linked teen accounts can set “quiet hours” when their teen can't access ChatGPT, and receive safety notifications in limited high-risk situations, such as the possibility of a user hurting themself.</p><p>“We are adding additional notifications related to eating disorders, while limiting what is shared and focusing on moments when offline support may matter most,” OpenAI said.</p><p>For homework help, OpenAI said the teen chatbot is designed not to give easy answers but to guide students to come up with answers on their own. The company already offers a version of ChatGPT for teachers, and tailoring a model to help kids with studying and homework could give OpenAI more ways to bring its product to schools.</p><p>“We continue to also invest in expanding interactive learning because research shows that people learn more effectively when they actively engage and struggle with concepts,” Mishkin said.</p>
entries.author: Barbara Ortutay | AP

entries.title: Man charged with sucker-punching fan at Cubs-Sox game at Wrigley Field
entries.summary: <p>A man was arrested and charged with punching a fan at Monday night's Crosstown Classic game at Wrigley Field, where the Cubs beat the White Sox 7-5 in extra innings.</p><p>The fight, which Chicago police say is not connected to an eighth-inning brawl in the stands captured in a <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/reels/DcLxaRWkZSj/" target="_blank" >widely shared video</a>, happened outside a restroom as the game was wrapping up, according to court records.</p><p>The 26-year-old victim told police that a man "sucker punched" him with his right fist, causing his nose to bleed, according to a police report.</p><p>Police arrested David Cregan, 41, of the Archer Heights neighborhood, around 10:43 p.m. and charged him with felony cocaine possession and misdemeanor battery, according to the report.</p><p>Police also reported two other arrests that night, both tied to trespassing — but no charges tied to the brawl in the stands.</p><p>The Cook County state's attorney's office did not immediately say whether it had reviewed charges related to the brawl.</p><p>After the game, the Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/17/cubs-white-sox-crosstown-series-playoffs-standings-nl-central-al-central-pete-crow-armstrong-seiya-suzuki" target="_blank" >told reporters</a> that the fight in the stands was "unfortunate and somewhat nauseating."</p><p><i>Contributing: Vinnie Duber</i></p>
entries.author: David Struett

entries.title: Ford City Mall developer modifies project plans ahead of first city hearing
entries.summary: <p>The developer that wants to transform the shuttered Ford City Mall into an industrial campus could receive its first city approvals this week, after broadening its plans to include a public plaza and new CTA bus stop.</p><p>Chicago-based Kurv Industrial, formerly Bridge Industrial, plans to demolish Ford City Mall and build a four-building<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/07/16/ford-city-mall-losing-shoppers-bridge-industrial-evolution" > industrial campus</a>. The project will be considered by the Chicago Plan Commission on Thursday.</p><p>Kurv’s plans submitted to the Plan Commission show a new Ford City heritage plaza that celebrates “over 80 years of Chicago history,” with landscaping and seating. It also shows a new CTA bus station along Kostner Avenue, east of the mall.</p><p>The plaza and bus station could make Kurv’s plans more appealing to commissioners. Warehouses and industrial plans often face steep community opposition for their lack of public use and spaces, along with concerns of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/05/12/warehouse-boom-next-day-delivery-die-80-amazon-centerpoint-intermodal-northpoint-joliet-manhattan-elwood" >increased traffic, noise and air pollution</a>.</p><p>Ald. Derrick Curtis (18th), whose ward includes the mall, said in a letter to constituents, posted on his website, that the mall’s closure represents “the end of an important chapter,” but it must also mark the beginning of something new and better. </p><p>“My priority is to ensure that this property does not remain neglected,” Curtis wrote. “We must pursue responsible redevelopment that protects our neighborhoods, creates economic opportunities, strengthens our tax base and brings productive new investment to the 18th Ward.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Cicero Ave. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Kurv was under contract to purchase Ford City Mall from Namdar Realty Group in July 2025; the buildings nearby like the AMC Ford City 14 movie theater weren't included in the deal. The developer announced plans to turn the Southwest Side mall into an industrial campus, zoned for warehousing or light manufacturing. Kurv estimated the redevelopment would cost $150 million — and it would need the City Council to sign off on rezoning the mall site from a shopping district to industrial.</p><p>Plans now put the redevelopment at $200 million, likely due to the new plaza, bus station and additional infrastructure work. Under the updated plans, 76th Street would be reconstructed as a public thoroughfare.</p><p>Kurv didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>The four buildings would vary in size, with the two largest spanning more than 300,000 square feet. The remaining two buildings are roughly 200,000 square feet and 100,000 square feet.</p><p>A traffic study conducted for the site found there would be “significantly less total traffic” at an industrial park compared to Ford City Mall.</p><p>The mall was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/05/15/ford-city-mall-southwest-side-judge-ordered-close-june-22" >ordered to close June 22</a>, following a court hearing. Greg Janes, assistant corporation counsel for the city of Chicago, said during the hearing that all parties in the case agreed to the June 22 shutdown. </p><p>Namdar Realty Group had previously been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/04/17/ford-city-mall-verge-shuttering-namdar-failure-repairs" >given seven days</a> to present a plan to either close the mall’s businesses or vacate the building, following its court-ordered shutdown. The company had failed to make repairs to the deteriorating mall, including fixing a malfunctioning fire suppression system and preventing constant flooding. There were also concerns about exposed wiring and possible sinkholes.</p><p>The forced closure came after years of declining sales. At the time of its closing, the mall had about two dozen retailers — including its last anchor tenant, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/04/24/jcpenney-backtracks-ford-city-shutdown-mall-peril" target="_blank" ><u>JCPenney</u></a>. Other stores included Foot Locker, Sam’s Furniture and Victoria’s Secret, though many merchants already left the mall prior to the court order.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/05/15/ford-city-mall-southwest-side-judge-ordered-close-june-22" >Ford City Mall on Southwest Side ordered to close by June 22</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/07/16/ford-city-mall-losing-shoppers-bridge-industrial-evolution" >Ford City Mall, losing its hold on shoppers, could see an industrial evolution</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bears training camp report No. 15: Can anybody cover TE Colston Loveland this season?
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ Tuesday training camp practice:</p><h3><b>Loveland dominates</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Tight end Colston Loveland has looked un-guardable for most of training camp, and that’s not simply because the Bears’ defense has been hit with injuries. At 6-foot-6, 241 pounds with great speed, defensive play callers are going to have trouble figuring out their personnel against him.</p><p>While it was another up-and-down day for quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>, he found Loveland in the back, right corner of the end zone from the 6-yard line. Cornerback Jaylon Johnson and linebacker Jon Rhattigan were trailing in coverage, and Johnson seemed to throw his hands up as if to say there was nothing he could do.</p><p>Loveland has emerged as the Bears’ biggest weapon, and he’s going to be especially valuable in tight spaces like the red zone.</p><h3><b>Hit and miss</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Williams continued his recent trend of some misfires, some great throws and an overall OK day — neither great nor terrible.</p><p>He hit wide receiver Khalif Raymond quite a bit, mostly underneath but also a beautiful lob to him on the right sideline for a 28-yard gain during a two-minute drill. However, Williams also overthrew Scotty Miller deep for a would-be touchdown during seven-on-seven work and threw a little behind Rome Odunze in the end zone and left the ball where defensive back William Wright could deflect it.</p><h3><b>Getting rough</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The most intense part of practice was a one-on-one special teams blocking drill in which the entire team circled around to watch. The highlights were wide receiver Jahdae Walker destroying rookie cornerback Malik Muhammad and defensive lineman Jeremiah Martin manhandling rookie tight end Sam Roush.</p><h3><b>Big auditions</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Bears mixed up their first- and second-string defensive players, ostensibly to give some backups a chance to prove themselves with the starters and vie for spots. Most notably, rookie defensive tackle Jordan van den Berg, a sixth-round pick, got a shot with the first team.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: MLB Field of Dreams game averages 1.66 million viewers on Netflix
entries.summary: <p>LOS ANGELES — MLB's first game at the Field of Dreams movie site in four years in Dyersville, Iowa, averaged 1.66 million viewers on Netflix on Thursday night, according to Nielsen.</p><p>The Philadelphia Phillies beat the Minnesota Twins 7-1 on two home runs by Kyle Schwarber.</p><p>This was the first year that Netflix has carried one of MLB's special event games. According to Nielsen, the average median age was 46, the youngest for an MLB special event game.</p><p>The first MLB game at the Field of Dreams site in 2021 between the White Sox and New York Yankees averaged 5.91 million on Fox while the Cubs-Cincinnati Reds matchup in 2022 averaged 3.10 million.</p><p>Last year's Speedway Classic in Bristol, Tennessee, between the Atlanta Braves and Cincinnati Reds averaged 1.6 million viewers on Fox. The game started on a Saturday night but went to Sunday due to rain.</p><p>The 2024 game at Rickwood Field in Birmingham, Alabama, between the San Francisco Giants and St. Louis Cardinals averaged 2.5 million on Fox.</p>

entries.title: QB Tyson Bagent joins list of Bears wounded in grueling preseason
entries.summary: <p>Add another name to the list of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ wounded: Tyson Bagent.</p><p>The backup quarterback did not practice Tuesday because of a hamstring injury suffered in Saturday’s 34-10 exhibition win against the Browns, a source said. The injury not considered serious — Bagent played every snap he was scheduled to Saturday and spoke to the media afterward — but it’s unclear if he’ll be ready to face the Bengals in four days.</p><p>At least that injury happened in the game.</p><p>The Bears have lost five prominent players to serious injury — one that lasts a week or longer — suffered during one of the team’s 15 training camp practices.</p><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson believes in holding grueling practices to get ready for the season. That’s not going to change.</p><p>“I think we've had some pretty physical practices, and I feel really good about where we're at,” he said before Tuesday's practice. “I thought it translated to that game. Our physicality showed up Week 1 on all three phases, so I'm pretty pleased with that right now.”</p><p>He acknowledged, though, the toll that such physicality can take. He said he and his staff are constantly trying to fine-tune their practice schedules. </p><p>“We turn the dial every single day,” Johnson said. “We look at what we're doing, how we're doing it and we always adjust and we're going to continue to do that.</p><p>“We have a method to what we're doing. Our guys believe in it. We believe in it and I feel really good about the path that we're on.”</p><p>Maybe it's just bad luck?</p><p>“There are things that you can't control sometimes,” he said.</p><p>Head coaches, though, need to be in control. In just his second season, Johnson needs to navigate a new challenge — how to get his starters to Week 1 when someone seems to get hurt in practice nearly every day. </p><p>That's more daunting than it was in Johnson's first training camp, when he held one legendarily violent practice to instill in his players what he wanted to see in games. When the Dolphins came to town for a joint practice last year, they were overwhelmed — and almost offended — by the Bears' physicality.</p><p>Johnson's players, though, weren’t getting injured in practice at this rate last year.</p><p>On Sunday, running back Kyle Monangai became the sixth prominent Bears player to suffer a serious injury during practice:</p><p>• Safety Coby Bryant, the team’s big-money free agent acquisition, who will miss most of the season after needing surgery on his knee. He suffered a hyperextension, bone bruise and break during an Aug. 3 practice.</p><p>• Wide receiver Luther Burden hurt his groin Aug. 8 when he and cornerback Tyrique Stevenson both jumped reached for a potential touchdown pass in one-on-one drills. He’s likely to return by the start of the season — and was seen sprinting before Saturday’s game.</p><p>• Defensive end Montez Sweat, who practiced in full for the first time since Aug. 6 on Sunday.</p><p>• Left tackle Braxton Jones, who was hurt the same day and has since returned from a knee injury.</p><p>• Cornerback Tyrique Stevenson missed practice Tuesday, marking a full week since he last participated in the Bears’ scrimmage.</p><p>• And Monangai, who is “week-to-week,” Johnson said Tuesday after hurting his knee Sunday when he became tangled with defensive tackle Grady Jarrett on a running play. Jarrett was distraught in the moment, though Johnson said he wasn't worried about him, calling him a "pro."</p><p>Even more standouts showed up to camp hurt.</p><p>Cornerback Kyler Gordon continues to rehab a calf injury that has somehow limited him for months. The Bears have done a terrible job hiding their frustration with the injury. For the second time in four days, Johnson was tight-lipped about Gordon when asked about his progress. He said there was “nothing to add” about his injury, before adding, vaguely, that “there’s a plan, and he’s working toward the plan.”</p><p>Starting Linebacker T.J. Edwards got a late start to camp after hurting his calf while training off-site. Ozzy Trapilo, the Bears’ starting left tackle, returned to practice Sunday in a shockingly fast recovery from a patellar tendon injury.</p><p>The injuries kept coming Tuesday, too, of course. Kiran Amegadjie, who along with Jedrick Wills was moved off of left tackle before practice, left with a trainer.</p><p>The Bears will hold a light practice Wednesday before flying to Cincinnati for a joint practice Thursday. Maybe then they'll be able to tell just how rough-and-tumble they've become — and whether it was worth it.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Triunfan los Cubs en clásico ante los White Sox con 2 jonrones del MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong
entries.summary: <p>Es el mundo de Pete Crow-Armstrong y el resto del béisbol solo vive en él.</p><p>Así se ha sentido muchas veces durante una temporada al nivel de jugador más valioso (MVP) del jardinero central de los Cubs, que puso otro gran signo de exclamación en su vitrina de galardones el lunes por la noche al conectar un par de jonrones, el segundo de los cuales resultó en una victoria por 7-5 con jonrón de desempate en la décima entrada sobre los White Sox, rivales de la misma ciudad.</p><p>El estacazo de Crow-Armstrong lo metió en el club de los 30-30 por segunda temporada consecutiva y le dio a los Cubs su duodécima victoria por jonrón de desempate en Wrigley Field.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0c0000" name="module-0c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>“Esto es lo que hacen los grandes jugadores”, dijo después el mánager Craig Counsell. “Hemos tenido varios de estos momentos a lo largo de la temporada con Pete. Es un momento de un gran jugador. Cumplen en situaciones como esta”.</p><p>El juego fue un clásico de ida y vuelta entre dos equipos con aspiraciones reales de postemporada.</p><p>“Es realmente genial que podamos poner ese espectáculo en el campo juntos y competir”, comentó Crow-Armstrong. “Es muy bueno para la ciudad que ambos estemos jugando el béisbol que jugamos y entregando partidos como el de esta noche”.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong abrió el marcador con el primer jonrón de la serie en la primera entrada, y Seiya Suzuki conectó el otro. En el cuarto, el abridor de los Cubs,Shota Imanaga<b>,</b> permitió su cuadrangular número 29 de la temporada, un jonrón de tres carreras del bateador designado Randal Grichuk que puso adelante a los Sox, solo para que los Cubs respondieran en la siguiente entrada, cuando anotaron dos con un rodado suave y un error en el tiro.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">PCA REACHES THE 30/30 MARK IN WALK-OFF FASHION. <a href="https://t.co/1JvfTLDk02">pic.twitter.com/1JvfTLDk02</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2089555460122677657?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Andrew Benintendi conectó un jonrón que dio vuelta al partido anteRyan Zeferjahn, la incorporación de los Cubs en la fecha límite de cambios, en el octavo, solo para que Nico Hoerner empatara en la parte baja de la novena antes del jonrón de desempate de Crow-Armstrong una entrada después.</p><p>Suma ese batazo a la lista cada vez mayor de grandes momentos entre Cubs y Sox, uno bastante grande como para destacarse en una temporada llena de ellos para Crow-Armstrong.</p><p>“No creo que haya conocido jamás a un jugador así”, dijo Imanaga a través de un intérprete. “Lo ves jugar, hacer las jugadas fantásticas que hace, y no te sorprende realmente. Pero las expectativas que uno pueda tener, o que un fan pueda tener sobre él, siempre las supera. Ha sido increíble”.</p><p>“Pete es mi MVP”, dijo el relevistaJacob Webb (5-2), quien se acreditó la victoria tras lanzar la décima entrada sin permitir carreras.</p><h3>Webb otra vez</h3><p>Webb amplió su racha de apariciones sin admitir carreras a 22.</p><p>“No ha sido un tipo que haya lanzado en la novena ni en estos momentos, y cuando lo ves lanzar, parece que lleva ahí desde hace 10 años”, dijo Counsell. “Ese es el sentido que tengo. No hay nadie a quien prefiera tener ahí fuera. Sigue impresionando cada vez que recibe la bola”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: NASCAR will not return to Grant Park in 2027
entries.summary: <p>The NASCAR street race will not return to Grant Park in 2027 after the clock ran out <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nascar/2026/06/02/nascar-2027-grant-park-chicago-street-race-may-return-earlier-in-summer" >on efforts to find an alternative date</a> outside the already-busy July 4th weekend and secure a $15 million state grant.</p><p>Downtown Ald. Brian Hopkins (2nd) said the surprise decision was “75% scheduling and 25% money.”</p><p>After receiving a $5 million state grant for each of the three years the Chicago Street Race was held, Hopkins said NASCAR officials made, what they thought was a strong case for a $15 million state tourism grant.</p><p>The state budget approved last spring renewed the $5 million grant.</p><p>Money was a “contributing factor” to the decision not to return to Chicago.</p><p>But Hopkins said the major reason was the demand by the city and local alderpersons that NASCAR hold the Chicago Street Race on an alternative summer weekend, and not further strain the Chicago Police Department and other city workers over the July 4th holiday.</p><p>“Had they been able to resolve the scheduling and logistics issues with the city, they would have gone forward without the full level of state support that they thought was ideal, but they ran out of time,” Hopkins said Tuesday.</p><p>“They had to announce their schedule. And the risk was, if they continued delaying this decision, they would potentially lose out on the ability to have it at the Joliet Speedway. So they had to take the sure thing. Joliet is there. It’s available. And what they’re saying is, this will be the Chicago Street Race that we know, just transported to Joliet. Same field of drivers. Same position in the NASCAR hierarchy. The event is unchanged except for the venue.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-170000" over.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times file </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Joliet race will be held June 25-27.</p><p>A source close to NASCAR confirmed the decision to shift to Joliet “wasn’t just about money.”</p><p>NASCAR “has to get its schedule out by the end of August” and “ran out of time” to nail down all of the details despite a “genuine good faith effort” to finalize an alternative Chicago weekend, the sources said.</p><p>The sources noted that, for every event NASCAR moves, the schedule for races in other cities must be altered as well.</p><p>NASCAR issued a statement that did not explain the reasons for the one-year shift to Joliet. But NASCAR made it clear the door remains open to a return to Chicago in 2028.</p><p>“We're incredibly grateful to the City of Chicago, the State of Illinois, Choose Chicago, the Chicago Sports Commission, our labor and business partners, community organizations, neighbors and, most importantly, our fans who made this first-of-its-kind event such a tremendous success,” the statement said.</p><p>“While we will not be racing on the streets of Chicago in 2027 despite genuine joint efforts by both NASCAR and our partners at the city and state level, we remain committed to the Chicagoland region and would welcome the opportunity to bring the NASCAR Chicago Street Race back at some point in the future."</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson's office likewise sounded a conciliatory note, saying the city was "proud to host NASCAR" and they "remain open to discussing the future of NASCAR in Chicago."</p><p>The statement continued: "The race provided an opportunity to showcase Chicago to a global audience and demonstrated the potential of our streets and downtown as a setting for major events. While NASCAR will not return to Chicago in 2027, we’re pleased that NASCAR has decided to maintain its Chicago office and continue investing in important community programs like NASCAR STEAM Fest with class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>For three years, the NASCAR Street Race drew a large and dedicated fan base that filled Chicago hotels and patronized the city’s restaurants — even though rain was a problem on several of the race days.</p><p>The nationally-televised event also showcased the beauty of the Chicago lakefront and downtown to a much broader audience that might be motivated to visit the city at a later date.</p><p>Illinois Restaurant Association President Sam Toia said his members were looking forward to welcoming the crowds he called “NASCAR tourists” back to Grant Park in 2027 on a weekend other than the already busy July 4th weekend.</p><p>That makes Tuesday’s announcement a big disappointment.</p><p>“Their fan base — this is like religion to them. Very, very strong fan base,” Toia said.</p><p>“Losing an event like this could be impactful in the summertime because independent restaurants live for the summertime. Not just the guests in beds and diners in seats, but the exposure we get from NASCAR on national television. … They see how beautiful Chicago is and then they want to come and visit Chicago.”</p><p>Michael Jacobson, president of the Illinois Hotel & Lodging Association, said hotel operators are a resilient bunch.</p><p>“When we lose an event like this, we’re able to find other events to fill that place and we did that this year. We had a very successful July 4th weekend this year as well,” Jacobson said.</p><p>“But NASCAR was looking to move to a weekend that had less demand that we could have used a boost in tourism during. That’s where working together to figure out what works for everybody is where the conversation moves to next. We’re hopeful that we can find a way to win them back in the future working together with a longer runway and a longer time line.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-420000" name="image-420000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5248240/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2Fbb%2F0191321fedf341d82fc25fa3fe36%2Fnascarsun-070323-34.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5a8eccc/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2Fbb%2F0191321fedf341d82fc25fa3fe36%2Fnascarsun-070323-34.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b259c12/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fc3%2Fbb%2F0191321fedf341d82fc25fa3fe36%2Fnascarsun-070323-34.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Fans cheer as the green flag is waved to start the race during the Grant Park 220 NASCAR Street Race, Sunday, July 2, 2023. Chicago “served as the launching pad” for a “history-making event” that transformed downtown streets into a “world-class racecourse.” It proved that a street race “could work in a major city."</p><p>“Although the race isn’t returning in 2027, Choose Chicago remains committed to working with our partners at NASCAR … in hopes of welcoming the race back to Chicago in future years,” the agency’s statement said.</p><p>Hopkins said he has asked NASCAR to use the time between now and 2028 to "minimize the disruption" to downtown Chicago by reducing the set-up and take-down time for a return to a Chicago Street Race in Grant Park "in coordination with the Suenos" music festival and other summer events.</p><p>"They said they were gonna do that anyway. But I said, `Now, you've got more time. Get creative and make it a top priority so that you can come back eventually with a new proposal in 2028 that will feature a reduced footprint at both ends — set-up and take-down,'" Hopkins said.</p><p>"That's been a major concern for my residents — even the ones that have supported this event. And I've had a divided constituency. It's been pretty close to 50-50. So if they want to win over even more downtown residents, that's the best way to do it."</p><p><i>Contributing: Kaitlin Washburn</i></p>
